newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian merger activity seen rising - study.
newsitem.headline: Australian merger activity seen rising - study.

text.p: Corporate merger activity is likely to increase in Australia during 1997, according to an analysis of the level of takeover activity in Australia undertaken by accounting group, Ernst & Young.

"We are already seeing evidence of an increase in the number of overseas players acquiring Australian corporates and this trend is likely to gain momentum throughout 1997," said Ernst & Young national mergers and acquisitions partner Peter Kempen in a statement accompanying the group's April Mergers and Acquisitions (M&A) Index study.
Kempen said the study found that merger activity had become more aggressive with companies undertaking larger acquisitions and willing to pay higher prices.

The M&A Index covers all acquisitions by listed industrial companies, including acquisitions of other listed companies, divisions and subsidiaries of listed companies, unlisted public companies and private companies.
The April index found that Australian companies spent more than A$12.5 billion on takeovers in calendar 1996, a 96 percent rise over 1995.
The study found most transactions took place off market with just 15 percent of deals involving one listed Australian company taking over another.
"The M&A Index trend reveals that deals are becoming fewer but bigger," Kempen said.
"The actual number of acquisitions in 1996 was lower than in 1994 or 1995, but the value of those deals was higher than in both those years put together," he said.
The study found the average acquisition price in 1996 was A$63.8 million compared to A$23 million between 1993 to 1995.

"The only limiting factor over recent mergers and acquisitions activity has been the shortage of sellers in Australia. That together with strong interest from overseas buyers, has pushed prices higher," Kempen said.

Kempen said this was reflected in an increase in the price asset ratio (PAR), which measures the total price paid compared with the net asset value acquired. The study found the PAR rose to 1.67 in 1996 from 1.37 in the previous year.
